body: Dosya auto-disables a webhook after 15 consecutive failed delivery attempts. Prove the receiver first: the test route can call a disabled endpoint without reopening normal event traffic. ## Steps 1. Open **Integrations → Webhooks** in the affected workspace and find the **Disabled** card with **Auto-disabled after repeated failures**. Note the reported failure count and disable time. 2. Repair DNS, TLS, routing, signature verification, durable queueing, and the response path. The URL must remain public HTTPS, and the receiver must answer with 2xx within ten seconds. 3. Select **Send test event** while the endpoint is still disabled. Dosya creates a signed `file.uploaded` sample and reports **Test event sent — Check the deliveries log below for the result.** 4. Open **Deliveries** and wait for that new row to show **Success**. The toast proves creation only; **Pending**, **Failed**, `Error`, or a non-2xx response means the receiver is not ready. 5. Select **Re-enable**. The server sets the endpoint active, clears `consecutive_failures`, removes `disabled_at`, and reports **Webhook re-enabled**. 6. Trigger one controlled subscribed event and verify another **Success**. Review older **Failed** rows separately because activation does not resurrect or replay them. The failure threshold counts attempts across the endpoint, so several broken events can reach 15 before one event exhausts its own six attempts. A successful test clears the active failure incident but does not itself set the disabled endpoint active. ## Expected result The receiver proves a successful signed request before future traffic resumes. The endpoint returns to **Active** with cleared failure state, and only explicitly redelivered historical events run again. **Re-enable failed** leaves the endpoint disabled. Reload the card, confirm the role still has `manage_settings`, and retry without repeatedly sending tests. **The endpoint disables again.** Inspect the most recent response status or transport error and stop re-enabling until the underlying receiver failure is corrected. ## Related guides - [Create a webhook](/developers/webhook-create) - [Inspect deliveries](/developers/webhook-deliveries)

title: Retry webhook deliveries safely
summary: Build transactional event-ID idempotency around Dosya’s six-attempt retry schedule so repeated requests change downstream state only once safely.
verification: Source-reviewed locally on 2026-10-14 against apps/api/src/lib/webhooks/deliver.ts, apps/api/src/lib/webhooks/retry.ts, apps/api/src/pages/api/webhooks/[id]/deliveries/[did]/redeliver.ts, apps/api/src/lib/webhooks/health.ts. Production behavior for “Retry webhook deliveries safely” was not exercised; this revision is awaiting publication.
body: Retries are normal delivery behavior, so the receiver must make one event safe to execute more than once. Dosya’s stable business identifier is the event ID; a delivery ID identifies an attempt record and can change during manual replay. ## Steps 1. Verify `X-Dosya-Signature` against the raw body and require matching `X-Dosya-Event-Id` and body `id` before entering the business transaction. 2. Insert the event ID into a uniquely constrained idempotency table inside the same transaction that applies the downstream mutation. Store processing status and a safe result reference for recovery. 3. On a unique-key conflict, read the committed result and return 2xx without repeating the mutation. Do not use `X-Dosya-Delivery-Id` as the sole key because **Redeliver** assigns a new one. 4. Commit durable work before acknowledging. A receiver crash before commit causes a safe retry; committing a side effect and its marker separately creates a window where the next attempt can duplicate state. 5. Exercise the failure path once. Dosya sends an initial attempt and, while failure continues, schedules five more after 30 seconds, 2 minutes, 10 minutes, 1 hour, and 6 hours; the sweep may run later than each due time. 6. Let the retry succeed and inspect **Deliveries**. Confirm one business result, one shared event ID, the attempt count, and **Success** with no next retry. Any 2xx ends retry. A non-2xx response, network error, disallowed redirect, or ten-second timeout increments the endpoint’s consecutive-failure counter; 15 such failed attempts auto-disable the endpoint. ## Expected result Repeated requests for the same event either create the single intended downstream result or return its committed result. Delivery attempts remain observable without becoming additional business actions. **The effect happened twice.** Move the idempotency claim and mutation into one atomic boundary, then repair existing duplicates before replaying the event. **A poison event retries repeatedly.** Quarantine its verified payload durably and choose a deliberate acknowledgement policy; returning failure consumes the six-attempt schedule and contributes to auto-disable. ## Related guides - [REST API quickstart](/developers/rest-api-quickstart) - [Inspect webhook deliveries](/developers/webhook-deliveries)

title: Rotate a webhook signing secret
summary: Roll a webhook signing secret, copy the one-time replacement immediately, update the receiver, and verify new signatures after the old key stops.
verification: Source-reviewed locally on 2026-10-14 against apps/web/src/pages/integrations/webhooks.tsx, apps/api/src/pages/api/webhooks/[id]/roll-secret.ts, apps/api/src/lib/webhooks/deliver.ts, apps/api/src/pages/api/internal/webhooks/retry.ts. Production behavior for “Rotate a webhook signing secret” was not exercised; this revision is awaiting publication.
body: Webhook secret rotation is an immediate cutover. Dosya does not overlap old and new secrets: the previous value stops verifying as soon as **Roll secret** succeeds, and the replacement is shown once. ## Steps 1. Prepare access to the receiver’s secret store and deployment path before changing Dosya. Pause unrelated receiver changes and choose a low-traffic window because the replacement cannot be known in advance. 2. Open **Integrations → Webhooks**, match the endpoint URL, and select **Roll secret**. Confirm your workspace role includes `manage_settings`; an API credential needs **Full access**. 3. In **Roll signing secret**, read `The old secret stops working immediately - update your receiver before rolling.` Choose **Roll secret** only when you can perform the cutover now. 4. In **Signing secret**, copy the new `whsec_…` value and store it securely. Dosya reports `Store it securely - you won't see it again.` and does not offer retrieval after the dialog closes. 5. Update and deploy the receiver, then remove the old value from its configuration. Pending retries read the endpoint’s current secret on their next attempt, so they will also arrive signed with the replacement. 6. Choose **Send test event**, open **Deliveries**, and require **Success** plus a valid new signature at the receiver. Investigate any requests that arrived during the short rotation window before resuming normal operations. Secret rolling is limited to ten requests per user per hour. The audit trail and integration notification identify the endpoint and actor but never store either secret. ## Expected result The receiver accepts deliveries signed with the one-time replacement and rejects the retired secret. New tests and later retries use the current secret, with no unsupported dual-secret period implied. **Roll secret failed** means no confirmed replacement was returned. Keep the current receiver configuration, reload the endpoint, and retry only after checking the rate limit. **The dialog closed before copying.** The value cannot be recovered. Roll again, copy the newly issued secret, and update the receiver promptly; the intermediate secret is already obsolete. ## Related guides - [Create a webhook](/developers/webhook-create) - [Inspect deliveries](/developers/webhook-deliveries)

title: Send a test webhook
summary: Send Dosya’s signed file.uploaded sample, inspect the receiver and Recent deliveries, and distinguish a queued test from a successful response.
verification: Source-reviewed locally on 2026-10-14 against apps/api/src/pages/api/webhooks/[id]/test.ts, apps/web/src/pages/integrations/webhooks.tsx, apps/api/src/lib/webhooks/deliver.ts, apps/api/src/lib/webhooks/retry.ts. body: A test is a real signed webhook delivery, but the immediate toast confirms creation rather than receiver success. Use the resulting row and receiver log as the delivery receipt. ## Steps 1. Open **Integrations → Webhooks**, select the workspace, and locate the intended endpoint by its full URL. The action requires a role with `manage_settings`; the test route is also available while an endpoint is disabled. 2. Prepare the receiver to capture safe identifiers and validate the current signing secret. Do not log the full request body or signature while testing. 3. Select **Send test event**. Dosya creates a `file.uploaded` event with `file_id: "test_file"`, `name: "test.txt"`, `size: 12`, `folder_id: null`, `version: 1`, `is_new_version: false`, and `test: true`. 4. Read **Test event sent — Check the deliveries log below for the result.** This means a `whd_…` row was created and its first attempt scheduled; it does not claim the endpoint returned 2xx. 5. Open **Recent deliveries** and inspect the new `file.uploaded` row. Match its `X-Dosya-Event-Id` and `X-Dosya-Delivery-Id` at the receiver, then require **Success**, a 2xx response, and the expected attempt count. 6. If the row is **Pending**, use **Next retry** rather than sending repeated tests. If it is **Failed**, fix the stored response or transport error, then create one new controlled test and verify it end to end. Each test can follow the normal six-attempt retry schedule and contributes to endpoint health failures. Dosya limits test creation to 20 requests per user in five minutes. ## Expected result One signed sample is visible at the receiver and reaches **Success** in **Recent deliveries**. Its fixed `test_file` payload is clearly distinguishable from a real upload, and no secret enters logs. **Test failed** means Dosya could not create the test request. Read the returned error, confirm permission and rate-limit state, and avoid treating the absence of a row as receiver failure. **The row shows Error.** Inspect DNS, TLS, public-HTTPS validation, redirect behavior, or timeout at the receiver; a transport error has no HTTP status. ## Related guides - [Create a webhook](/developers/webhook-create) - [Inspect deliveries](/developers/webhook-deliveries)

title: Verify Dosya webhook signatures
summary: Validate the X-Dosya-Signature timestamp and HMAC against the untouched request body, reject replayed requests, and rotate exposed secrets safely.
verification: Source-reviewed on 2026-10-14. Verified the header format, HMAC input, SHA-256 output, one-time secret display, raw request delivery and rotation behavior in apps/api/src/lib/webhooks/sign.ts; apps/api/src/lib/webhooks/sign.unit.test.ts; apps/api/src/lib/webhooks/deliver.ts; apps/api/src/lib/webhooks/deliver.unit.test.ts; apps/api/src/pages/api/webhooks/[id]/roll-secret.ts; apps/web/src/pages/integrations/webhooks.tsx; and src/pages/developer/api.astro. Local repository evidence only; no production request was made.
body: Verify every webhook before parsing its JSON or starting work. Dosya signs the exact request body with the endpoint's `whsec_` secret and sends the result in `X-Dosya-Signature`. A valid signature proves possession of that secret; it does not replace authorization checks your downstream job may require. ## Signature contract The header has this exact shape: ```text t=UNIX_SECONDS,v1=64_LOWERCASE_HEX_CHARACTERS ``` Compute `HMAC-SHA256(secret, timestamp + "." + raw_body)` and compare the 32-byte digest to `v1` using a constant-time operation. `raw_body` means the untouched HTTP entity bytes. Parsing and reserializing JSON, changing whitespace, normalizing Unicode, or converting line endings produces a different digest. Use the `t` value for replay protection. Dosya's API reference recommends rejecting a signature more than **300 seconds** away from the receiver's current time. Keep receiver clocks synchronized and evaluate the timestamp before enqueuing the event. The five-minute test is performed by your receiver; Dosya does not know whether your application enforced it. ## Steps Configure the route to expose a `Buffer` containing the original body. Framework JSON middleware often consumes or transforms it, so apply raw-body handling to this route before a global JSON parser. ```javascript import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto'; export function verifyDosya(rawBody, signatureHeader, secret, nowSeconds) { const match = /^t=(\d+),v1=([0-9a-f]{64})$/.exec(signatureHeader ?? ''); if (!match) return { ok: false, reason: 'malformed signature' }; const timestamp = Number(match[1]); const now = nowSeconds ?? Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000); if (!Number.isSafeInteger(timestamp) || Math.abs(now - timestamp) > 300) { return { ok: false, reason: 'stale timestamp' }; } const expected = createHmac('sha256', secret) .update(match[1] + '.') .update(rawBody) .digest(); const received = Buffer.from(match[2], 'hex'); const valid = received.length === expected.length && timingSafeEqual(received, expected); return valid ? { ok: true, timestamp } : { ok: false, reason: 'signature mismatch' }; } ``` Pass a `Buffer`, not an already parsed object, as `rawBody`. After the function returns `ok: true`, parse JSON, require the expected top-level `id`, `type`, `created`, `workspace_id`, and `data`, then write the event ID into a unique deduplication store. Return 2xx after that durable acceptance. Dosya retries non-2xx responses and timeouts, so a receiver that authenticates correctly can still see the same event again. ## Test the positive and negative paths 1. Open [Integrations → Webhooks](https://app.dosya.dev/integrations/webhooks) for a controlled endpoint and select **Send test event**. 2. Confirm the receiver accepts the signed request and records the `X-Dosya-Event-Id`, `X-Dosya-Delivery-Id`, event type, and timestamp. Do not log the signature or secret. 3. In a local test, alter one byte of the captured body while keeping the header unchanged. Verification must fail before JSON processing. 4. Test a different secret, a missing header, malformed hex, and a timestamp 301 seconds outside the allowed window. None may enqueue work. 5. Redeliver the valid event and prove the unique event-ID constraint prevents a duplicate downstream action. The **Success** badge in Dosya means your endpoint returned 2xx. It cannot prove your receiver checked the signature. Keep a receiver-side test for valid and invalid cases as the deciding evidence. ## Diagnose signature mismatches | Symptom | Correction | | --- | --- | | Every delivery fails after deployment | Ensure the route receives bytes before JSON or form middleware and uses the secret for this exact endpoint. | | Only non-ASCII or formatted payloads fail | Remove text decoding and reserialization from the HMAC input; hash the received bytes. | | Valid traffic is marked stale | Synchronize the receiver clock and compare Unix seconds rather than milliseconds. | | Old captured requests still pass | Add the 300-second timestamp window and persist event IDs. | | Failures began immediately after **Roll secret** | Install the newly revealed secret; the previous one stops validating new deliveries immediately. | The secret appears in **Signing secret** only when the endpoint is created or rotated. Losing it requires **Roll secret**; the old value stops working without an overlap period. The rotation endpoint allows 10 calls per user per hour, and the new value is returned once. If a secret reaches source control, logs, screenshots, or chat, rotate it rather than deleting only the exposed copy. ## Expected result A current, untouched request signed with the saved endpoint secret is accepted. Missing, malformed, stale, altered, or wrongly signed requests are rejected before they change state, and a repeated valid event is acknowledged without repeating its business effect. ## Related guides - [Create and test the endpoint](/developers/webhook-create) - [Inspect delivery status and retries](/developers/webhook-deliveries) - [Rotate a signing secret](/developers/webhook-rotate-secret)

title: Troubleshoot failed Dosya webhook deliveries
summary: Diagnose webhook reachability, signatures, timeouts, HTTP responses, retries, auto-disablement, duplicates, redelivery, and secret rotation.
verification: Source-reviewed 2026-10-14 against apps/web/src/pages/integrations/webhooks.tsx; apps/api/src/pages/api/webhooks/[id]/test.ts; apps/api/src/pages/api/webhooks/[id]/deliveries/index.ts; apps/api/src/pages/api/webhooks/[id]/deliveries/[did]/redeliver.ts; apps/api/src/lib/webhooks/deliver.ts; apps/api/src/lib/webhooks/retry.ts; apps/api/src/lib/webhooks/sign.ts; apps/api/src/lib/ssrf-guard.ts. No external receiver was contacted. Local repository evidence only; no production request was made.
body: Use the endpoint's **Deliveries** table and the receiver log for the same delivery. The table identifies event, creation time, status, response, attempts and next retry; the receiver should log the nonsecret event and delivery IDs. Never diagnose a signature failure by turning verification off on a production endpoint. ## Steps 1. Open **Integrations → Webhooks** in the workspace that owns the endpoint. 2. Confirm the card is **Active** and includes the expected event: `file.uploaded`, `file.deleted`, or `share.accessed`. 3. Expand **Deliveries**, open the failed row and record its event type, delivery/event identifiers, response status, attempts, next retry, error and sanitized response snippet. 4. Compare the row's attempt time with your receiver and edge/proxy logs. No incoming request points to URL/DNS/SSRF validation, connectivity or an upstream proxy; an incoming request with rejection points to receiver verification or processing. Webhook administration requires workspace membership plus **manage_settings**. Built-in owners and administrators qualify. A missing Webhooks control or 403 **You don't have permission to manage webhooks** must be fixed through the workspace role; rotating a key does not widen that member permission. ## Match the failure to the receiver boundary | Symptom | Recovery | | --- | --- | | URL creation/edit returns **Endpoint URL not allowed: …** | Use a public HTTPS receiver. Localhost, private-network and disallowed DNS/address targets are rejected at registration and delivery. | | Receiver gets no POST | Verify the saved URL, public DNS and TLS, proxy route, firewall and whether the endpoint is Active. Check for a recorded URL-validation error in the delivery. | | Receiver returns 3xx | Configure the final stable HTTPS URL. Dosya follows at most one allowed redirect; a second redirect is recorded as failure. | | Delivery times out | Acknowledge after authentication and durable queueing. The receiver has 10 seconds; perform long work asynchronously. | | Response is 4xx/5xx | Read receiver logs for `X-Dosya-Delivery-Id`; correct that route and return any 2xx only after acceptance. Every non-2xx is a failed attempt. | | Signature mismatch | Verify the untouched request bytes with the endpoint's current `whsec_…` secret. Do not parse/reformat JSON before computing HMAC. | | Endpoint says **Auto-disabled after repeated failures** | Fix and test the receiver, then choose **Re-enable**. Re-enabling clears the consecutive-failure counter but does not repair old failed work. | | Event processed twice | Deduplicate on the envelope event `id`. Retries keep that event identity; a manual redelivery creates a new delivery row for the same event/payload. | Dosya signs `timestamp + "." + raw_body` with HMAC-SHA256. The header is `X-Dosya-Signature: t=TIMESTAMP,v1=LOWERCASE_HEX_HMAC`. Compare the digest in constant time and reject timestamps more than 300 seconds from your receiver clock. Also record `X-Dosya-Event-Id`, `X-Dosya-Event-Type`, and `X-Dosya-Delivery-Id`; none of those headers is a replacement for signature verification. If **Roll secret** was used, the old secret stopped working immediately. Update the receiver with the newly revealed value; there is no overlap period. A lost reveal requires another rotation. Keep signatures and secrets out of request logs. ## Understand retry timing A delivery has six total attempts: the first runs immediately, followed after failures by 30 seconds, 2 minutes, 10 minutes, 1 hour and 6 hours. Scheduling/network work can add delay. After the sixth failed attempt the delivery stays failed. Fifteen consecutive failed attempts across events auto-disable the endpoint. Any successful attempt resets that consecutive run. Re-enable only after a controlled test can succeed, or the endpoint will begin failing again. The receiver response body retained in Dosya is limited to 500 characters. Return a short neutral acknowledgement; credentials, stack traces and private content should not be copied into that response. ## Send a controlled test Select **Send test event**. This creates a synthetic `file.uploaded` event whose data includes `test: true`, file ID `test_file`, name `test.txt`, and size 12. It is sent even if the endpoint subscribes only to another event, so the receiver should recognize the test flag rather than treating it as production content. The toast **Test event sent** confirms only that the test was queued. Refresh **Deliveries** and wait for **success**, then verify the receiver stored exactly one authenticated event. Test and manual-redelivery routes each allow 20 calls per user per 300 seconds; a 429 response supplies a `Retry-After` to honor. After the synthetic test, trigger one harmless event that the endpoint actually subscribes to. Confirm the event's workspace and payload metadata, then check that downstream work happened once. ## Redeliver safely Use **Redeliver** only after checking whether the original request already changed downstream state. A timeout or lost response can leave the receiver successful while Dosya recorded failure. Search by event ID first, make the handler idempotent, and then queue one redelivery. The UI message **Redelivery queued — A new delivery attempt has been scheduled.** is not the final delivery result; inspect the new row. Deleting the endpoint permanently removes its delivery history and cannot recall payloads already received. Preserve nonsecret evidence before deletion. Secret rotation is also immediate and irreversible for the old secret. ## Expected result A fresh test delivery reaches the intended HTTPS endpoint, passes raw-body signature verification once, returns a successful response before the timeout, and does not create a duplicate side effect. ## Escalate with correlated evidence Provide the endpoint ID, event and delivery IDs, event type, UTC/local attempt time, response status, attempt count, sanitized snippet/error, receiver framework, and whether the request reached your edge and application. Do not include the signing secret, full signature, authorization headers, private payload fields or credentials. ## Related guides - [Create a webhook](/developers/webhook-create) - [Verify signatures](/developers/webhook-signatures) - [Inspect deliveries](/developers/webhook-deliveries)

title: Troubleshoot a failed WordPress backup
summary: Read the exact WordPress backup error, distinguish a local backup from a failed cloud upload, correct the cause, and retry the same scope safely.
verification: Source-reviewed locally on 2026-10-14 against apps/wordpress/src/Wp/Admin/ViewModel/StatusCard.php, apps/wordpress/src/Wp/Admin/ListPayload.php, apps/wordpress/src/Wp/Admin/ViewModel/BackupRow.php, apps/wordpress/src/Remote/RemoteStage.php, apps/wordpress/assets/js/api.js. Production behavior for “Troubleshoot a failed WordPress backup” was not exercised; this revision is awaiting publication.
body: A failed run can stop before any usable backup exists, or it can finish the local archive and fail only while sending that archive to Dosya. The Backups status card and row badges distinguish these cases, so preserve the error text before retrying. ## Steps 1. In WordPress wp-admin, open **dosya Backup → Backups**. You need an administrator on a single site, or a network administrator on multisite; other roles cannot run or inspect jobs. 2. Read the status headline and choose **View log**. Record the backup time, requested scope, and exact error. A row labeled **Failed · …** has no restorable archive; **dosya · upload failed** means the local archive exists and only its off-site copy failed. 3. Fix the named cause before another run. Restore disk space for archive errors, restore outbound HTTPS for Dosya errors, or reconnect if the Dosya tab says **Connection to dosya lost** or **This site was disconnected from dosya.dev**. 4. If storage is nearly full, review exclusions or capacity first. The plug-in warns at 90% usage; once full, the next upload is skipped and its backup remains on this server only. 5. Choose **Retry now** once. The status card repeats the failed run’s `full`, `db`, or `files` scope; it does not silently change the requested contents. 6. Keep the page open while the job advances. Requests poll about every 300 ms, slow to 3 seconds while busy, and retry a dropped connection after 1, 3, then 10 seconds before showing a failure. Do not delete the last good backup while diagnosing the failure. Incomplete working directories older than 24 hours are cleanup candidates, but completed local backups follow the separate **Keep on this server** setting. ## Expected result The new row completes with **local**, **dosya · not verified**, or **dosya · verified** instead of a failure badge. An upload-only failure still leaves the local row downloadable and restorable; retry after connectivity returns. A later successful backup clears the persistent failed-backup status. ## Related guides - [Connect WordPress](/integrations/wordpress-connect) - [Manage backups](/integrations/wordpress-backups)

title: Understand protected WordPress backups
summary: Read the exact lock deadline on a WordPress backup, understand which site key is restricted, and wait before deleting protected cloud backup data.
verification: Source-reviewed locally on 2026-10-14 against apps/api/src/lib/wp/repo.ts, apps/api/src/pages/api/wp/backups/[id]/complete.ts, apps/wordpress/src/Wp/Admin/ViewModel/BackupRow.php, apps/wordpress/src/Wp/Admin/Ajax.php, apps/wordpress/src/Jobs/LocalStore.php, apps/wordpress/src/Wp/Admin/ViewModel/ConnectCard.php, and apps/api/src/pages/api/wp/connect/exchange.ts. Production behavior for “Understand protected WordPress backups” was not exercised; this revision is awaiting publication.
body: Every completed remote WordPress backup receives a `locked_until` time. While that time is in the future, the site key cannot delete or change the protected copy, and the Backups row shows **🔒 until …**. ## Steps 1. Open **dosya Backup → Backups** in wp-admin and find the remote row by its created time and note. 2. Confirm the row is stored off-site: it must show **dosya · not verified** or **dosya · verified**. A **local** row has no Dosya protection deadline. 3. Read the **🔒 until …** badge and its tooltip. The displayed deadline uses the WordPress site timezone and states only when the remote backup-folder lock expires. The site key’s route restrictions remain in force afterward; expiry does not grant a change or delete route. 4. Treat that deadline as a Dosya cloud control. It does not lock the separate archive stored on the WordPress server, and the badge makes no claim about folders belonging to earlier referenced backups. 5. If the deadline is still future, leave the copy in place. Disconnecting the site revokes its key but keeps stored backups; it does not shorten an existing lock. 6. Keep wp-admin **Delete** separate from the cloud lock. It removes the local backup directory and checks only for newer local dependents; it neither waits for the badge to expire nor deletes the protected remote folder. A new connection currently starts with 24 hours of protection. The plan model exposes higher protection ceilings, but the row deadline and the Dosya tab’s **Protection** fact are the authoritative values for this connection. ## Expected result The row displays the exact deadline for its remote backup-folder lock, and the site credential cannot change that cloud folder early. Local wp-admin deletion remains a separate operation governed by local incremental dependencies, not by the remote protection clock. ## Related guides - [Manage WordPress backups](/integrations/wordpress-backups) - [Review backup status](/integrations/wordpress-review-backup-status)

title: Understand WordPress backup retention
summary: Compare local backup count with the remote expiry date, preserve incremental dependencies, and know which WordPress copy will remain available.
verification: Source-reviewed locally on 2026-10-14 against apps/wordpress/src/Wp/SettingsSchema.php, apps/wordpress/src/Wp/Admin/templates/schedule.php, apps/wordpress/src/Jobs/LocalStore.php, apps/wordpress/src/Jobs/BackupJob.php, apps/wordpress/src/Remote/RemoteStore.php, apps/api/src/lib/wp/repo.ts, apps/api/src/pages/api/wp/backups/[id]/complete.ts, and apps/api/src/pages/api/wp/connect/exchange.ts. body: WordPress keeps local backups by count and remote backups by an expiry timestamp. These are independent policies: a local prune does not prove the Dosya copy expired, and remote expiry does not change the plug-in’s local count. ## Steps 1. Open **dosya Backup → Schedule** and read **Keep on this server**. The accepted local count is 1 through 30; the default for a new install is 3. 2. Open the **dosya** tab and read **Retention** for the connected site. New connections in the current release initialize at 7 days, even when the account plan exposes a higher retention ceiling. 3. Return to **Backups** and compare each created time with the two policies. Remote completion sets `expires_at` from the site’s stored retention days. 4. Run a successful backup before expecting local pruning. The local store prunes after success and retains any older backup that a kept incremental still references. 5. Do not delete an older full merely because its date exceeds the simple count. The UI refuses deletion when one or more newer backups depend on it and names the dependent count. 6. If a later row is full, treat that as an automatic chain restart. The plug-in chooses full when no usable previous remote manifest exists, the base chain is at least 30 days old, the earlier list is unavailable, required local volumes are missing, or the reference ceiling is exceeded; wp-admin has no force-full control. The local setting removes older completed backups only after a successful run. Source review found the API assignment of `expires_at`, but no local production sweeper contract that guarantees immediate deletion at that second. ## Expected result You can identify which copies are governed by the local count and which carry a remote expiry. Necessary incremental bases remain local while referenced, and the remote record exposes its expiry date without promising an exact physical-deletion minute. ## Related guides - [Manage WordPress backups](/integrations/wordpress-backups) - [Review backup status](/integrations/wordpress-review-backup-status)

title: Manage WordPress backups
summary: Start scoped WordPress backups, read local and Dosya states, inspect logs and downloads, and understand retention before safely deleting a copy.
verification: Source-reviewed 2026-10-14; no production backup, restore, or deletion was run. body: Use the WordPress **Backups** tab to start a database-and-files, database-only, or files-only job and to distinguish the copy on your server from the copy stored in Dosya. ## Steps 1. In wp-admin, open **dosya Backup**. Only a single-site administrator (`manage_options`) or multisite network administrator (`manage_network_options`) can use these controls. 2. On **Backups**, read the status card before starting another job. **No backup yet**, **Backed up on this server**, **Uploading to dosya**, **Uploaded to dosya, not yet verified**, and **Verified restorable** describe different checkpoints. 3. Press **Back up now**, then choose **Database and files**, **Database only**, or **Files only** under **What to back up**. 4. Optionally fill **Note (optional)**. The plug-in keeps at most 80 characters and shows the note beneath the backup's creation time. 5. Select **Start backup**. One backup or restore may run at a time; the page disables competing start actions while the job advances in short resumable steps. 6. Wait for the result banner, then find the row by **Created** and **Type**. The table also reports **Contents**, **Size**, and **Stored**; it shows 20 rows per page with **Newer backups** and **Older backups** pagination. 7. Treat **local** as “stored on this server only.” Prefer **dosya · verified** before depending on the off-site copy. **dosya · not verified**, **dosya · uploading**, and **dosya · upload failed** need more attention. 8. Open **More actions** for **Download manifest**, numbered `v0001.dosya` volume downloads, **View log**, or **Delete**. An incremental download needs its earlier chain; use a full backup for migration. The first remotely stored backup is full. Later jobs may become incremental when the earlier uploaded chain is eligible; the row says `incremental, new`. Volume size defaults to 64 MiB and is validated from 16 through 256 MiB. Local retention is 1–30 backups, while the visible Schedule choices are 3, 5, and 10 unless another saved value exists. ## Expected result A completed row identifies its scope and byte size, and its **Stored** badge tells you whether the recoverable copy exists locally, is still transferring, or has been verified by Dosya. The footer totals every backup and byte kept on this WordPress server. ## Resolve a failed or blocked action - **Last backup failed: _cause_** keeps the previous good backup visible. Choose **View log**, correct the reported cause, and use **Retry now**; retry repeats the failed scope. - **dosya connection lost, uploads paused** means the local backup can still exist, but off-site transfer needs **Connect again**. - **A backup or restore is running.** Wait for that job to end before deleting another local backup. - A disabled **Delete** names how many newer incremental backups depend on the selected base. Remove those dependents first. Deleting from this page removes the server copy; its Dosya copy is kept. - Automatic jobs may run later than the selected clock time because WP-Cron starts on a site visit. **Backup overdue** appears only after 1.5 schedule intervals, when a whole run has effectively been missed. ## Related guides - [Connect WordPress](/integrations/wordpress-connect) - [Understand storage usage](/uploading/storage-usage)

title: Connect a WordPress site to a Dosya workspace
summary: Approve a WordPress site for one Dosya workspace, understand the confined site key, and confirm its folder, retention, and protection facts.
verification: Source-reviewed locally on 2026-10-14 against apps/web/src/pages/connect/wordpress.tsx, apps/api/src/lib/wp/connect.ts, apps/api/src/pages/api/wp/connect/authorize.ts, apps/api/src/pages/api/wp/connect/exchange.ts, apps/wordpress/src/Wp/Connector.php, apps/wordpress/src/Wp/Admin/ViewModel/ConnectCard.php, and apps/wordpress/readme.txt. body: The connection flow grants one WordPress installation a dedicated `wp_site` key confined to a newly created site folder. It does not give the plug-in general access to the workspace. ## Steps 1. Confirm WordPress 6.0 or later, PHP 7.4 or later, a MySQL or MariaDB connection, and 64-bit PHP. Sign in to the Dosya account that belongs to the target workspace. 2. In wp-admin open **dosya Backup → dosya** and select **Connect to dosya**. The browser approval request expires after 15 minutes on the WordPress side. 3. On **Save backups in workspace**, choose the intended workspace. The selector lists every workspace membership and defaults to the active workspace when present, otherwise its first row; it does not pre-filter rows by backup permissions. 4. Read the grant and choose **Allow** once. Authorization separately requires both `create_folders` and `upload_files`; an insufficient role returns **You don't have permission to back up a site into this workspace** and creates no connection. An accepted site key is confined to its new `WordPress Backups` site folder. 5. Return to wp-admin within the one-time exchange window. The authorization code lasts 5 minutes and cannot be reused; an expired attempt says **This connect link expired or was already used. Start again.** 6. Confirm **Connected to dosya** and record the **Folder**, **Retention**, and **Protection** facts. Then run one manual backup and wait for an off-site badge. The site sends its address, name, and backup data to Dosya. If PHP sodium is unavailable, the plug-in warns that the saved site key is stored unencrypted in the WordPress database. ## Expected result The site has its own confined credential and unique folder under `WordPress Backups`, and the Dosya tab names the account and workspace. Current connections initialize with 7-day retention and 24-hour protection; the displayed facts control, even if the plan page shows higher ceilings. ## Related guides - [Connect WordPress](/integrations/wordpress-connect) - [Manage WordPress backups](/integrations/wordpress-backups)

summary: Connect dosya Backup from wp-admin, choose an allowed workspace, approve the site, and verify its restricted backup key, folder, and status.
verification: Source-reviewed 2026-10-14; no production site was connected. body: Connect the dosya Backup plug-in from WordPress, choose where its off-site copies belong, and approve a credential made specifically for that site. The connection never asks for your WordPress administrator password. ## Before you connect - The plug-in requires WordPress 6.0 or newer, PHP 7.4 or newer, 64-bit PHP, and MySQL or MariaDB through `mysqli`. It does not require PHP's ZIP extension. - In a single-site installation, sign in with a role that has WordPress's `manage_options` capability. For multisite, use a network administrator with `manage_network_options`. - The Dosya account approving the request must be an unconfined member of the chosen workspace with both `create_folders` and `upload_files`. A folder-confined member cannot place the site folder at the workspace root. - The plan controls active sites, retention, and protection: Free is 1 site / 7 days / 24 hours; Starter 3 / 30 / 72; Plus 10 / 90 / 168; Pro 25 / 180 / 336; Business unlimited / 365 / 720. ## Steps 1. In wp-admin, open **dosya Backup**, select the **dosya** tab, and press **Connect to dosya**. 2. If Dosya asks you to sign in, complete sign-in in that browser. Do not reuse a bookmarked connect URL: WordPress keeps the pending request for 15 minutes, and the one-time approval code itself lasts 5 minutes. 3. On **Connect _host_ to dosya**, compare the site name and host with the WordPress installation you started from. 4. Under **Save backups in workspace**, choose the intended workspace. The page shows the plan's site count, retention days, and immutability hours. 5. Press **Allow**. Dosya creates `WordPress Backups/ ()`; if that name exists, it uses `(2)`, `(3)`, or another available suffix. 6. After the browser returns to wp-admin, look for **Connected to dosya**. Confirm the account, workspace, **Folder**, **Retention**, and **Protection** facts before running a backup. The issued site key can write to that site's backup folder and register its backups. It cannot browse the rest of the workspace, overwrite a backup, or delete a protected copy. ## Expected result The wp-admin card says **Connected to dosya**, identifies the selected workspace and site folder, and offers **Open in dosya ↗** plus **Disconnect**. A first backup can now stay on the server and upload a second copy to the displayed folder. ## If connection fails - **Your plan's connected site limit is reached.** Disconnect an unused site or choose a plan with a higher site cap. - **You don't have permission to back up a site into this workspace.** Ask a workspace administrator for folder-creation and upload permissions, or choose a workspace where you already have them. - **This connect link expired or was already used. Start again.** Return to the plug-in's **dosya** tab and begin a fresh request. - **This connect link does not match the request this site started. Start again.** Use the same wp-admin session and its newest browser tab; the state belongs to one request. - **The site's folder in dosya no longer exists. Connect the site again.** Approving again creates a new site folder and a new restricted key; it does not restore the deleted folder. - **Connecting was cancelled. Nothing was changed.** Restart only when you are ready to approve the listed site and workspace. ## Related guides - [Connect a cloud account](/integrations/connect-cloud-account) - [Contact support](/troubleshooting/contact-support)

title: Respond to a WordPress copy-detected warning
summary: Resolve a WordPress copy-detected warning by identifying the clone, stopping new backups, and connecting the installation that should continue.
verification: Source-reviewed locally on 2026-10-14 against apps/api/src/pages/api/wp/sites/[id]/heartbeat.ts, apps/api/src/pages/api/wp/backups/index.ts, apps/wordpress/src/Wp/Connector.php, apps/web/src/pages/integrations/wordpress.tsx, apps/wordpress/src/Wp/Admin/ViewModel/ConnectCard.php. body: Dosya identifies a WordPress installation with a stored fingerprint. If the same credential reports a different site or home URL, the service marks that connection **Copy detected, check the site** to prevent a clone from silently writing into the original site’s backup chain. ## Steps 1. In Dosya open **Integrations → WordPress** and note the row labeled **Copy detected, check the site**. Record its site name, URL, workspace, and last backup before changing either installation. 2. Determine whether the URL changed because of an intentional migration, a staging clone, or an unexpected database copy. Do not let both installations keep the same saved site key. 3. Pause scheduled backups on the copy that should not own the connection. A clone-suspected site may report status and may finish a backup already in progress, but the API rejects every new backup registration. 4. On the installation that should continue, open **dosya Backup → dosya** and disconnect the copied credential if it remains readable. Stored Dosya backups are retained. 5. Choose **Connect again**, approve the intended workspace, and let the flow create a fresh confined connection. Reconnection can create a newly suffixed site folder; it does not merge the old chain. 6. Run one manual backup from the intended installation. Verify its new site row and folder, then separately retain or remove the old site connection only after confirming the new copy. A copy warning is a credential-identity safeguard, not proof of compromise. Preserve both URLs and the last successful timestamps if the copy was unexpected. ## Expected result Only the intended WordPress installation can register new backups with its new credential. The prior remote backups remain in their original folder, and the new connection begins its own chain instead of silently attaching clone data to the old record. ## Related guides - [Manage WordPress backups](/integrations/wordpress-backups) - [Review backup status](/integrations/wordpress-review-backup-status)

title: Disconnect a WordPress site safely
summary: Revoke one WordPress site's restricted key, stop later off-site uploads, preserve stored backups, and understand how to reconnect safely when needed.
verification: Source-reviewed 2026-10-14; disconnect was not executed on a production site. Claims checked against apps/web/src/pages/integrations/wordpress.tsx; apps/web/src/pages/integrations/wordpress.test.tsx; apps/api/src/pages/api/wp/sites/[id]/disconnect.ts; apps/api/src/pages/api/wp/sites/[id]/disconnect.unit.test.ts; apps/wordpress/src/Wp/Connector.php; apps/wordpress/src/Wp/Admin/AdminPage.php; apps/wordpress/assets/js/dosya.js; and apps/wordpress/src/Wp/SiteKeyStore.php. Illustrations show the confirmed decision flow.
body: Disconnecting revokes the site's restricted Dosya key and prevents later off-site uploads. Backups already stored in Dosya, their folder, database rows, and active protection locks remain in place. ## Steps 1. Decide which control matches your access. The account that connected the site can use Dosya **Integrations → WordPress**; a WordPress administrator can use **dosya Backup → dosya** from that installation. 2. Before disconnecting, verify the exact site name and host. Open its folder and confirm at least one usable stored copy if off-site recovery matters. 3. In Dosya, open **Actions for _site_**, choose **Disconnect**, and read **Disconnect _site_ from dosya? Backups already stored in dosya are kept.** In wp-admin, press **Disconnect** and read the equivalent site-level warning. 4. Choose **Cancel** to leave the connection intact, or press **Disconnect** to proceed. 5. In the web app, wait for **Site disconnected** and `_site_ is no longer connected. Its backups are kept.` The row is removed from the active list. 6. In wp-admin, the page reloads after the request. The connection card returns to **Store copies in dosya** with **Connect to dosya**. ## Expected result The API key is deleted, its cache entry is invalidated, and the connected-site record becomes disconnected. Existing remote backup records, files, folders, and locks are retained; local backups on the WordPress server are untouched. The credential revocation cannot be undone. Reconnecting authorizes a newly issued site key and may create another uniquely suffixed site folder, so confirm the new **Folder** fact rather than assuming it reused the retained directory. ## Failure and recovery behavior - **Disconnect failed** in Dosya means the server did not confirm revocation; keep the dialog state and retry after checking the connection. - From wp-admin, the plug-in first tries to abort an open remote upload and disconnect remotely, then clears the locally stored key even if that remote call fails. If the page returns to **Store copies in dosya**, reconnect before expecting another off-site copy. - If Dosya later reports **This site was disconnected from dosya.dev**, select **Connect again**. The backups already held by Dosya remain safe while uploads are paused. - Disconnecting does not cancel WordPress's local schedule. Scheduled jobs can continue creating server-only backups until you set **Automatic backups** to **Off** on the **Schedule** tab. ## Related guides - [Connect WordPress](/integrations/wordpress-connect) - [Manage WordPress backups](/integrations/wordpress-backups)

title: Understand full and incremental WordPress backups
summary: Tell full and incremental WordPress backups apart, understand their dependency chain, and learn why a later valid run may become full again.
verification: Source-reviewed locally on 2026-10-14 against apps/wordpress/src/Jobs/BackupJob.php, apps/wordpress/src/Remote/RemoteStore.php, apps/wordpress/src/Wp/Admin/ViewModel/BackupRow.php, apps/wordpress/src/Wp/Admin/ListPayload.php, apps/api/src/pages/api/wp/backups/[id]/complete.ts. Production behavior for “Understand full and incremental WordPress backups” was not exercised; this revision is awaiting publication.
body: A full backup writes all selected database and file content. An incremental can reuse unchanged rows from earlier stored volumes and writes only changed data, so it depends on the backups it references. ## Steps 1. Open **dosya Backup → Backups** and compare the **Type**, **Contents**, **Size**, and **Stored** columns for two completed runs. 2. Read an incremental row’s contents hint, such as **incremental, 38 MB new**. The main size is the restore set; the hint is the newly written portion. 3. Expect the first connected backup to be full. Database-only runs, local-only runs, and runs without a usable previous remote manifest also stay full. 4. For an incremental, the plug-in must still see the prior backup and every referenced backup as uploaded or verified, find their local volumes, and keep the base full younger than 30 days. 5. If Dosya cannot list earlier backups, the new row records **dosya could not be reached to check the earlier backups, so this backup is a full one.** A chain that exceeds the reference ceiling also restarts full. 6. Before deleting any base, check the action refusal. The list disables deletion and states how many newer backups depend on that row; delete dependents first only when you intend to remove the chain. Backup scope and backup kind are different. **Database**, **Files**, and **Database + files** describe contents; full or incremental describes whether stored volumes reuse earlier data. ## Expected result Each row identifies its effective backup kind and newly stored bytes. A full fallback remains a valid independent backup; an incremental remains restorable only while its referenced local and remote chain is retained. ## Related guides - [Manage WordPress backups](/integrations/wordpress-backups) - [Review backup status](/integrations/wordpress-review-backup-status)

body: Every approved WordPress connection receives its own folder beneath `WordPress Backups`. Open it from the connected-site row so similarly named sites do not lead you to the wrong backup set. ## Steps 1. Use the Dosya account that originally approved the site and open **Integrations → WordPress**. 2. Under **Your WordPress sites**, match both the bold site name and the smaller host. This prevents confusion between production, staging, and cloned installations. 3. Select **Open folder** on that row. The control exists only when the connected-site record has a `root_folder_id`; it opens Dosya Files with that folder selected. 4. Check the breadcrumb and folder name. Connection creates `WordPress Backups/ ()`; a collision receives `(2)`, `(3)`, or a later free suffix rather than reusing another site's directory. 5. Inspect the ordinary files in that location. Compare backup timestamps and sizes with the WordPress **Backups** tab before downloading or restoring a set. 6. For the same destination from wp-admin, open **dosya Backup → dosya** and choose **Open in dosya ↗**. Its **Folder** fact should agree with the web-app destination. ## Expected result Dosya Files opens the root assigned to the chosen WordPress site, and the visible site-folder path matches the connection you inspected. Opening the folder is read-only by itself; it does not start a backup, restore WordPress, or alter retention. ## If Open folder is missing or wrong - A missing **Open folder** means the site list did not receive a root-folder ID. Refresh the page, then inspect **dosya Backup → dosya** in wp-admin for **The site's folder in dosya no longer exists. Connect the site again.** - If you signed in with another workspace member, the site may not appear because this page lists sites for the Dosya account that connected them. - If the folder was deleted, reconnecting creates a fresh restricted key and a new uniquely named directory. It cannot reconstruct the removed files. - If the host or site name is unexpected, stop before downloading or restoring anything and resolve a possible clone warning from the connected-sites table. ## Related guides - [Connect WordPress](/integrations/wordpress-connect) - [Manage WordPress backups](/integrations/wordpress-backups)

body: Install **dosya Backup 0.3.0** using its official ZIP in WordPress, then connect the site to Dosya if you want off-server backup copies. Installation, authorization and the first backup are separate checks. You can make local backups without a Dosya account; cloud upload requires the site connection. ## Check the site and download The plug-in requires **WordPress 6.0+**, **PHP 7.4+**, **64-bit PHP** and a **MySQL or MariaDB connection through mysqli**. Use a WordPress administrator allowed to install/activate plug-ins. On multisite, install/manage it through network administration; the Dosya admin page uses `manage_network_options`, versus `manage_options` on a single site. A hosting service that disables plug-in uploads must enable that capability before you can follow the ZIP procedure. Download [dosya-backup.zip](https://dosya.dev/downloads/wordpress/dosya-backup.zip). Use this official manual-install package rather than a similarly named search result. Keep the ZIP compressed for WordPress upload. Its top-level folder is `dosya-backup`, containing `dosya-backup.php` and the bundled job scheduler. A fresh activation enables a **daily 03:00** backup schedule in the site's WordPress timezone. Review **Schedule** promptly if you want a manual-only installation. Defaults also keep **3 local backups**, use **64 MiB** archive volumes, enable a restore safety copy and failure emails, and leave success emails off. The retention setting can keep **1–30** local backups and the archive volume setting accepts **16–256 MiB**. These local settings are separate from cloud retention. ## Steps: install and activate 1. In wp-admin open **Plugins → Add New Plugin** (called **Add New** in some WordPress versions), then **Upload Plugin**. 2. Choose `dosya-backup.zip`, click **Install Now**, wait for installation to finish and choose **Activate Plugin**. On multisite, use the corresponding network activation control. 3. Open the **dosya Backup** admin menu. If you plan to connect before any backup, first inspect **Schedule** and turn automatic backups off until setup is complete. Otherwise a local-only backup can run before the connection exists. 4. Confirm the version in the plug-in list. If activation fails, address the exact requirement instead of repeatedly installing the same archive. Two activation errors are **dosya Backup needs 64-bit PHP.** and **dosya Backup needs a MySQL or MariaDB database connection.** These deactivate the plug-in rather than leaving it usable. Ask your host to correct PHP architecture or database configuration. A corrupt/incomplete ZIP or failed scheduler dependency should be replaced with a fresh official package. ## Connect the site to cloud storage 1. In **dosya Backup → dosya**, click **Connect to dosya**. Sign in on the Dosya browser page and review the site URL/name and workspace. 2. Pick a workspace in which your Dosya membership can **create folders** and **upload files**. Folder-confined memberships cannot create the site folder at the workspace root. A local/private site address is not a valid cloud-connected site URL. 3. Approve the site and return to wp-admin. The authorization uses a one-time code protected by the site's PKCE challenge; you do not paste an account API key into WordPress. The site stores its dedicated credential encrypted using the site's security keys. 4. Confirm **Connected to dosya**, the account/workspace and **Folder** on the connection card. **Open in dosya ↗** lets you inspect that destination. The WordPress side keeps the pending connection for **15 minutes**; once approved, the exchange code lives **5 minutes** and is single-use. If the flow is interrupted, restart from Connect to dosya rather than resubmitting the old callback. Dosya receives the site's address, its name and backups you make. Backups can include database content and site files; configure exclusions or encryption before storing data you do not intend to upload. Each site gets a no-delete credential restricted to its backup folder. It does not grant the WordPress server ordinary account-wide REST, WebDAV or S3 access. Backups are stored under **WordPress Backups** in the approved workspace and consume Dosya storage. The effective account plan caps connections and cloud retention/protection as follows; the current connection card shows the configured values. | Plan | Connected sites | Maximum retention | Maximum lock after upload | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Free | 1 | 7 days | 24 hours | | Starter | 3 | 30 days | 72 hours | | Plus | 10 | 90 days | 168 hours | | Pro | 25 | 180 days | 336 hours | | Business | Unlimited | 365 days | 720 hours | Cloud locks prevent overwrite/deletion until expiry, including from your own account. Do not upload a test containing confidential data if you expect to delete it immediately. A **Your dosya plan does not allow another connected site.** message means free a connection slot or change the plan before trying again. ## Verify the result with a first backup In **Backups**, choose **Back up now**, select **Database and files** for a whole-site check and click **Start backup**. Keep the page open while checking progress. Background work runs through the bundled Action Scheduler; the open admin page can also advance work when background/loopback execution is unavailable. A queued job is not evidence that bytes reached Dosya. Wait for a completed row and inspect its **Stored** status. **dosya · verified** means Dosya confirmed every volume. **dosya · not verified** means upload occurred but volume confirmation is pending. A local-only row remains on your server; if upload failed or storage is full, it is not an off-server recovery copy. Use Open in dosya to check the destination and keep a downloaded backup for an independent restore test before relying on it. In **Schedule**, choose off, daily or weekly and verify the next-run display. WordPress scheduled execution depends on the host/cron reaching the scheduler, so 03:00 is the target time, not a guaranteed completion time. Review exclusions, local retention and failure email delivery; scheduled work skips a slot if another job is running. Restoring is a separate, destructive operation that can overwrite the current site's database/files—do not use Restore just to verify installation. ## Recover a setup problem | Message/state | Recovery | | --- | --- | | **This connect link expired or was already used. Start again.** | Start a fresh connect flow from wp-admin and return promptly after approval. | | **This connect link does not match the request this site started. Start again.** | Use the same site/browser request; abandon the stale callback. | | **Could not reach dosya to finish connecting. Please try again.** | Check the host's outbound HTTPS, then start again. | | **Connection to dosya lost** after site security keys change | Click Connect again. The old encrypted credential cannot be read with new salts; existing cloud backups remain safe. | | **The site's folder in dosya no longer exists. Connect the site again.** | Reconnect after investigating who removed that folder. | | **Session expired** during an admin action | Reload/sign in to wp-admin for a fresh session and action nonce. | | Job stuck or upload failed | Read **Log**, check local disk, scheduler/cron and network, and inspect the actual backup row before starting another job. | ## Upgrade, deactivate and remove For a manual ZIP upgrade, save a working backup first and upload the fresh official ZIP through the same Plugins screen, confirming WordPress's replacement of the existing plug-in. The code upgrades its job tables by version; existing settings and connection are retained. An older installation without saved settings does not acquire the fresh-install daily schedule merely through this upgrade. Deactivation removes scheduled backups and queued steps; it retains plug-in settings, job data and the connection. Reactivation enables the stored schedule again. **Disconnect** revokes the remote site connection when reachable and forgets the local credential; an open upload is aborted best-effort. The confirmation says **Backups already stored in dosya are kept.** If remote revocation could not reach Dosya, review the connected site there too. Deleting the plug-in's code has no custom uninstall cleanup for saved settings/job tables or backups. Treat removal and data deletion as separate tasks: disconnect first, keep recovery copies, then explicitly manage local/cloud backups and their locks. Local-only backups do not survive loss of this server merely because the plug-in was once active. ## Expected result WordPress lists dosya Backup as active, the configured schedule matches your intention and the first cloud copy is marked verified in the selected workspace. Installation alone is not a verified backup. ## Related guides - [Connect a WordPress site](/integrations/wordpress-connect) - [Manage WordPress backups](/integrations/wordpress-backups)

title: Update the Dosya WordPress plug-in
summary: Update the Dosya WordPress plug-in safely, confirm its database upgrade completed, and test the preserved schedule and workspace connection.
verification: Source-reviewed locally on 2026-10-14 against apps/wordpress/dosya-backup.php, apps/wordpress/src/Wp/Plugin.php, apps/wordpress/src/Wp/SettingsSchema.php, apps/wordpress/readme.txt, apps/web/src/pages/integrations/wordpress.tsx. Production behavior for “Update the Dosya WordPress plug-in” was not exercised; this revision is awaiting publication.
body: The current repository release identifies itself as dosya Backup 0.3.0. On version change, the plug-in installs or upgrades its job table and retains existing settings; a site that never saved settings is left with automatic scheduling off rather than unexpectedly gaining daily backups. ## Steps 1. Before updating, open **dosya Backup → Schedule** and record schedule, time, local keep count, exclusions, safety-copy choice, and email choices. Record the connected workspace and folder from the **dosya** tab. 2. Confirm the server still meets WordPress 6.0+, PHP 7.4+, 64-bit PHP, and MySQL or MariaDB requirements. Make a usable site backup before changing plug-in code. 3. Use **Plugins → Add New → Upload Plugin** with the official `dosya-backup.zip`, or use the normal WordPress update control when the same package is offered. Do not delete plug-in data to perform an update. 4. Distinguish activation from a later version migration. Activation failures—including non-64-bit PHP where `PHP_INT_SIZE < 8`, unsupported database support, or job-table installation—deactivate the plug-in and stop with `wp_die`. During ordinary `plugins_loaded` initialization, a version-migration table failure instead records an init error and leaves the plug-in idle for that request. 5. Reopen **dosya Backup** and verify the saved schedule and connection facts. If **Connection to dosya lost** appears, reconnect rather than pasting or copying the site key. 6. Run one manual database backup, then inspect its final badge and log. This test exercises job-table access, archive creation, and the existing remote credential with limited data. Deactivation removes scheduled and queued Action Scheduler hooks, so do not leave the plug-in inactive when automatic backups are expected. The update itself does not verify that an old backup can restore; keep the pre-update copy. ## Expected result The updated plug-in loads, retains the intended saved configuration, and completes a controlled backup. A version migration records the new plug-in database version only after job-table installation succeeds. ## Related guides - [Connect WordPress](/integrations/wordpress-connect) - [Manage backups](/integrations/wordpress-backups)

title: Reconnect a disconnected WordPress site
summary: Reconnect a WordPress site after revocation or lost local keys, preserve existing cloud backups, and verify a fresh confined upload path safely.
verification: Source-reviewed locally on 2026-10-14 against apps/wordpress/src/Wp/Admin/ViewModel/ConnectCard.php, apps/wordpress/src/Wp/Connector.php, apps/api/src/pages/api/wp/connect/authorize.ts, apps/api/src/pages/api/wp/connect/exchange.ts, apps/api/src/pages/api/wp/sites/[id]/disconnect.ts. Production behavior for “Reconnect a disconnected WordPress site” was not exercised; this revision is awaiting publication.
body: Reconnection is required when the saved site key was revoked or can no longer be decrypted after WordPress security keys changed. Existing Dosya backups remain safe, but uploads pause until a new approval completes. ## Steps 1. Open **dosya Backup → dosya** and identify the state. **Connection to dosya lost** means local security keys changed; **This site was disconnected from dosya.dev** means the remote key was revoked. 2. Record the old folder, last upload, retention, and protection facts if they are still visible. Do not delete old backup files while recovering access. 3. Choose **Connect again**, sign in to the intended Dosya account, and select **Save backups in workspace** for the correct workspace. 4. Choose **Allow** once and return promptly. The authorization code is single-use and expires in 5 minutes; the WordPress pending request expires after 15 minutes. 5. Confirm the new **Connected to dosya** card. The flow creates a new site credential and may create a uniquely suffixed site folder, so do not assume it reattaches the earlier remote chain. 6. Start one manual backup and wait for **dosya · not verified** or **dosya · verified**. Use **Open in dosya ↗** to confirm the new folder before changing the retained old copy. If the browser returns **This connect link expired or was already used. Start again.**, begin a new approval from wp-admin. Do not reuse the URL or a code from a different browser session. ## Expected result Uploads resume through a fresh credential confined to its site folder. Previously stored backups remain in Dosya and are not deleted by disconnect or reconnect, while the new connection starts from its own current full backup. ## Related guides - [Connect WordPress](/integrations/wordpress-connect) - [Manage backups](/integrations/wordpress-backups)

title: Review WordPress backup status
summary: Read each connected site's latest backup, stored bytes, warning state, and protection deadline without mistaking upload for completed verification.
verification: Source-reviewed 2026-10-14; no production backup was started or changed. Claims checked against apps/web/src/pages/integrations/wordpress.tsx; apps/web/src/pages/integrations/wordpress.test.tsx; apps/api/src/pages/api/wp/sites/index.ts; apps/api/src/pages/api/wp/sites/[id]/backups.ts; apps/api/src/lib/wp/types.ts; and apps/api/src/lib/plans.ts. The diagrams are explanatory artwork, not live-account screenshots.
body: Dosya's WordPress integration page gives the account that connected a site a cross-site status view. Use it to find stale, failed, unverified, or protected backups before opening wp-admin for recovery work. ## Steps 1. Sign in to Dosya with the account that approved the WordPress connection, then open **Integrations → WordPress**. 2. In **Your WordPress sites**, identify the row by its **Site** name and host. The page loads at most 20 sites; if more exist, it says **Showing 20 of _total_ sites.** 3. Read **Last backup**. **None yet** means no returned backup; **Uploading…** means the newest job is running; **Failed** includes when it occurred. A successful row shows relative time plus `full, ` or `incremental, new`. 4. Compare **Stored**. Dosya displays the total bytes from the first uploaded or verified backup in the returned history. **None** means no such copy was found; **Unknown** means that site's backup-history request failed. 5. Read **Status** independently of the size. Possible labels are **No backup yet**, **Last backup failed**, **Copy detected, check the site**, **Protected until _date and time_**, **Connected**, or **Unknown**. 6. Check the plan line above the table: **_count_ of _limit_ on your plan · _days_-day retention · _hours_ h protection**. Stored sizes use binary byte formatting, while protection deadlines use an exact local date and time. 7. If the row needs investigation, open that site's wp-admin **dosya Backup → Backups** screen. The web overview intentionally does not start, restore, download, or delete backups. ## Expected result You can name the site's newest backup condition, the bytes reported for a stored copy, and whether any retained backup is still protected. A green **Connected** status alone does not assert that the newest upload was verified. ## Interpret unusual states - **Unknown** under **Last backup**, **Stored**, or **Status** means Dosya could list the site but could not load that site's backups. Refresh once; if it remains, inspect wp-admin and the plug-in log. - **Copy detected, check the site** takes priority over backup state. Review the clone warning before allowing the copied installation to upload under the original identity. - **Protected until _date_** uses the latest lock end found in the returned backups. During that window the site's restricted key cannot change or delete the protected remote copy. - **Last backup failed** does not erase an earlier completed backup. Open the WordPress log to find the failure and verify the older row before retrying. ## Related guides - [Connect WordPress](/integrations/wordpress-connect) - [Manage WordPress backups](/integrations/wordpress-backups)

title: Fix a WordPress site limit error
summary: Resolve a WordPress connected-site limit by counting active sites, disconnecting the correct unused row, or increasing account plan capacity.
verification: Source-reviewed locally on 2026-10-14 against apps/api/src/lib/plans.ts, apps/api/src/lib/wp/repo.ts, apps/api/src/pages/api/wp/connect/authorize.ts, apps/web/src/pages/connect/wordpress.tsx, apps/web/src/pages/integrations/wordpress.tsx, apps/api/src/pages/api/wp/sites/[id]/disconnect.ts. Production behavior for “Fix a WordPress site limit error” was not exercised; this revision is awaiting publication.
body: A WordPress connection consumes one active site slot. The authorization page checks the plan cap transactionally, so simultaneous approvals cannot exceed it; disconnected sites no longer count, while their stored backups remain. ## Steps 1. In Dosya open **Integrations → WordPress** and read the plan line above **Your WordPress sites**. It shows the active count and finite cap; Business reports no numeric maximum. 2. Use the current plan limits as a diagnostic: Free 1, Starter 3, Plus 10, Pro 25, and Business unlimited active WordPress sites. 3. Identify an unused site by URL, status, and last backup. The web table renders at most 20 rows and says **Showing 20 of N sites** when more exist, so avoid assuming the visible set is the total. 4. If removing one, open its actions and choose **Disconnect**. Confirm the named site; this immediately revokes its API key but keeps existing backups and folder data. 5. Otherwise change the account plan before retrying approval. On the connect page, a full account reports **Your plan’s connected site limit is reached. See plans to connect more sites.** 6. Restart **Connect to dosya** from the intended WordPress installation and approve once. Confirm that the new site appears and that the plan count increased by one. Only an account owner’s signed-in browser can approve the connection; impersonated sessions are refused. The approval endpoint is also limited to 10 requests per 15 minutes and returns a retry delay when throttled. ## Expected result The intended site connects within the active-site allowance. A disconnected site frees a slot without erasing its prior backups, and a failed over-cap approval creates neither a usable site key nor a partial site connection. ## Related guides - [Connect WordPress](/integrations/wordpress-connect) - [Manage backups](/integrations/wordpress-backups)

title: Troubleshoot WordPress backup status that will not load
summary: Separate a failed WordPress site-list request from one site’s backup-list failure, preserve evidence, and retry without disconnecting healthy sites.
verification: Source-reviewed locally on 2026-10-14 against apps/web/src/pages/integrations/wordpress.tsx, apps/api/src/pages/api/wp/sites/index.ts, apps/api/src/pages/api/wp/sites/[id]/backups.ts, apps/wordpress/src/Wp/Admin/ViewModel/ConnectCard.php. Production behavior for “Troubleshoot WordPress backup status that will not load” was not exercised; this revision is awaiting publication.
body: The WordPress integration page makes one request for sites and then one backup-list request per displayed site. A top-level failure and a row with unknown backup details therefore have different causes and should not trigger the same recovery. ## Steps 1. Open **Integrations → WordPress** while signed in and copy the exact alert. **Could not load your WordPress sites. Please try again.** means the site-list request itself failed. 2. If the table loads but one row shows **Unknown** or blank stored details, record that site ID and URL. The page converts a failure of that site’s backup request to an unknown row while leaving other sites visible. 3. Reload once after confirming the browser is online. Do not disconnect a site merely to refresh status; disconnect revokes its credential and is not a status reload. 4. Check whether the account session expired. The sites route returns **Sign in required** for an unsigned session, **Site not found** for a missing record, and **You can only view your own sites** for another owner. 5. Compare the same site in wp-admin. Its **dosya** tab shows whether the local key is connected, unreadable, or revoked; the Backups list remains the source for the local archive. 6. If only one row still fails, preserve the request status and response body for support. If every row fails, preserve the top-level alert, account, time, and browser before signing in again. The page fetches backup details for only the first 20 displayed sites. A **Showing 20 of N sites** notice means additional active sites exist even though their backup rows were not requested on that view. ## Expected result The page either repopulates the account’s active site rows and their newest backup states, or the evidence identifies whether the account-wide sites request or one site-specific backups request failed. No healthy connection is revoked as a refresh tactic. ## Related guides - [Connect WordPress](/integrations/wordpress-connect) - [Manage backups](/integrations/wordpress-backups)

title: Verify a completed WordPress backup
summary: Confirm a WordPress backup completed locally, distinguish uploaded from remotely verified, and run an optional local volume integrity check.
verification: Source-reviewed locally on 2026-10-14 against apps/wordpress/src/Wp/Admin/ViewModel/BackupRow.php, apps/wordpress/src/Wp/Cli.php, apps/wordpress/src/Archive/VolumeReader.php, apps/api/src/pages/api/wp/backups/[id]/complete.ts, apps/wordpress/src/Wp/Admin/ListPayload.php. Production behavior for “Verify a completed WordPress backup” was not exercised; this revision is awaiting publication.
body: A completed archive, a successful upload, and remote verification are three distinct states. Use the row’s action availability and storage badge first, then use WP-CLI when you need to validate the local volume bytes. ## Steps 1. Open **dosya Backup → Backups** and locate the row by created time, note, type, and contents. A failed row has no Restore or Download action and is not a completed backup. 2. Confirm its local receipt: a normal completed row lists size and volume downloads and offers **Restore**. **local** means the copy exists only on this WordPress server. 3. Read the remote badge. **dosya · uploading** is unfinished; **dosya · not verified** means upload completion was accepted but Dosya has not confirmed every volume; **dosya · verified** is the remote verification receipt. 4. If command-line access is available, run `wp dosya list` to copy the exact backup ID, then run `wp dosya verify `. This reads every local volume and checks its SHA-256 and archive structure. 5. Treat **N volumes verified.** as local integrity evidence only. **Volume N is missing or damaged.** names the first local volume that fails; it does not change the remote badge. 6. For recovery confidence, keep the row and its dependencies, and perform a controlled restore test on a disposable installation. Verification does not prove the restored application behaves correctly. Remote completion validates up to 2,000 volumes and 2,000 references, checks that files are live and in the correct folders, checks sizes, and accepts references only to uploaded or verified backups from the same site. ## Expected result The backup has a usable completed local row, a clearly identified remote state, and—when WP-CLI was run—a local volume-integrity receipt. You know whether the copy is local-only, uploaded but awaiting verification, or remotely verified. ## Related guides - [Manage WordPress backups](/integrations/wordpress-backups) - [Review backup status](/integrations/wordpress-review-backup-status)

title: Reading workspace activity and audit details
summary: Filter the workspace activity log, expand an event for forensic details, and understand which records and names your role can see.
verification: Reviewed the current Activity page, filters, pagination, expanded event details and visibility gates against the local current web app, API and activity visibility tests on 2026-10-12. Screenshot events use isolated representative data.
body: The workspace activity log helps an authorized member answer who performed an action, what resource it affected, when it happened and, when available, where the request came from. Use it to investigate unexpected changes, confirm administrative work or narrow a support report. The compact **Recent activity** panel on Team shows a few events. Open **Activity** for filters, pagination and expandable details. ## Before you start - Select the workspace you want to investigate. - Your role needs **View activity log** and access to the Activity page. - A folder-restricted member cannot open the workspace-wide activity log. - Write down the approximate time, member, resource name or action you are looking for. - Activity records are evidence of recorded requests. They do not replace checking the current file, member or link state. ## Steps: find an event 1. Open **Activity** from the workspace navigation or the **All** link beside a dashboard activity panel. 2. Check the total activity count under **Activity log**. 3. Open **Category** and select one or more areas, such as files, sharing, team or authentication. 4. Open **Member** to narrow results to one or more actors. 5. Open **Action** to select exact event types. Choosing a category narrows the available actions. 6. Review the resulting rows. Each row names the actor, action, resource and relative time when that information is available. 7. Use the page controls at the bottom to move through older events. 8. Select **Clear filters** to return to the complete view. ## Steps: inspect event details 1. Select an activity row to expand it. 2. Read **When** for the absolute timestamp and relative age. 3. Review **Where** when a source IP and approximate location are available. 4. Review **Device** for the parsed browser and operating system. 5. Check **Source** to distinguish web and supported integration or protocol activity. 6. Check **Outcome** for success, failure or denial. 7. Review **Resource**, **Request** and **Session** identifiers when shown. These values help private support locate related records. 8. Select the row again to collapse it. ## Expected result The log shows activity your role is allowed to inspect, ordered with recent events first.
